summary.text: Couple the evolutions from masses \(n\) and \(n+1\) by tracking their unique extra particle, which stays or moves one cell right according to the parity of its current cell; mass conservation, contiguous support, and the evolution of the leading block of \(1\)s show that when the former stabilizes, this particle is in position \(n-1\) or \(n-2\). In the first case it reaches the new terminal cell after one update and in the second after two, while the coupling and absence of internal zeros exclude stabilization any earlier.

full_proof.text:
Let a configuration be represented by a function
\[
c:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N
\]
with finite support, where \(c(i)\) is the mass in cell \(i\). Extend every finite list of cell masses by zeros to the right. In this representation one step of the cellular automaton is the map \(F\) given by
\[
(Fc)(0)=\left\lceil\frac{c(0)}2\right\rceil,
\qquad
(Fc)(i)=\left\lceil\frac{c(i)}2\right\rceil+
\left\lfloor\frac{c(i-1)}2\right\rfloor\quad(i\geq1).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(Fc)(i)=\frac{c(i)+1}{2}+
\begin{cases}
0,&i=0,\\
c(i-1)/2,&i>0,
\end{cases}
\]
where the divisions on the right are integer divisions. Let
\[
C_n^t=F^t C_n^0,
\qquad
C_n^0(i)=\begin{cases}n,&i=0,\\0,&i>0,\end{cases}
\]
and let
\[
U_n(i)=\begin{cases}1,&i<n,\\0,&i\ge n.\end{cases}
\]
Thus \(U_n\) is the stable configuration consisting of \(n\) unit cells. Direct substitution shows that
\[
F(U_n)=U_n. \tag{1}
\]

We first establish the structural facts needed to know that stabilization occurs and that this functional model gives the sequence in the question.

A configuration has support bounded by \(N\) if \(c(i)=0\) for every \(i\ge N\). The initial configuration has support bounded by \(1\), and if the support of \(c\) is bounded by \(N\), then the support of \(Fc\) is bounded by \(N+1\). Hence
\[
C_n^t(i)=0\quad\text{for all }i\ge t+1. \tag{2}
\]
The total mass is preserved. Indeed, if \(c\) is supported below \(N\), then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i=0}^{N}(Fc)(i)
&=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\left\lceil\frac{c(i)}2\right\rceil
 +\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\left\lfloor\frac{c(i)}2\right\rfloor\\
&=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}c(i).
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows inductively that every \(C_n^t\) has total mass \(n\).

Reachable configurations also have no internal zero: if a cell is nonzero, every cell to its left is nonzero. This is true initially. To see that it is preserved, first note that a positive zeroth cell remains positive. For an index \(i>0\), if \((Fc)(i+1)>0\) but \((Fc)(i)=0\), the latter equality forces both \(c(i)=0\) and \(c(i-1)=0\). The positivity at \(i+1\) then forces \(c(i+1)>0\); but the old no-internal-zero property applied to \(c(i+1)>0\) contradicts \(c(i)=0\). Thus the property is preserved.

For \(n>0\), this implies the stronger support bound
\[
C_n^t(i)=0\quad(i\ge n). \tag{3}
\]
For if \(C_n^t(i)>0\), the no-internal-zero property makes all cells \(0,1,\ldots,i\) positive. Their total mass is then at least \(i+1\). Since the total mass is \(n\), one must have \(i<n\).

It is useful to identify the first place where a configuration ceases to be a string of ones. Define
\[
L_n(t)=\min\{i:C_n^t(i)\ne1\}.
\]
This minimum exists because the configuration has finite support. Thus
\[
C_n^t(i)=1\quad(i<L_n(t)),
\qquad C_n^t(L_n(t))\ne1. \tag{4}
\]
If \(C_n^t\ne U_n\), then
\[
C_n^t(L_n(t))\ge2. \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, if this cell were zero, the no-internal-zero property would force every cell from \(L_n(t)\) onward to be zero. The total mass would then be exactly \(L_n(t)\), contributed by the preceding ones. Hence \(L_n(t)=n\), and the configuration would be exactly \(U_n\), a contradiction. Since the leading cell is neither zero nor one, it is at least two. Conversely, these facts show that a reachable configuration of positive total mass equals \(U_n\) exactly when all of its cell masses are at most one.

We next prove that stabilization actually occurs. For a finitely supported configuration define its positional potential
\[
P(c)=\sum_{i\ge0} i\,c(i).
\]
If \(c\) is supported below \(N\), a direct reindexing gives
\[
P(Fc)=P(c)+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\left\lfloor\frac{c(i)}2\right\rfloor. \tag{6}
\]
This simply says that each unit of mass sent to the right increases the potential by one. If a reachable configuration is not stable, (5) supplies a cell of mass at least two, so the last sum in (6) is at least one. Thus the potential strictly increases by at least one at every nonstable step. On the other hand, by (3), every mass unit lies at an index less than \(n\), and the total mass is \(n\), so, for example,
\[
P(C_n^t)\le n^2. \tag{7}
\]
If stabilization never occurred, after \(t\) steps the potential would be at least \(t\), contradicting (7) when \(t>n^2\). Therefore there is at least one \(t\) with \(C_n^t=U_n\).

The finite-list automaton in the definition of \(a(n)\) is equivalent to this functional automaton. Extending a list by zeros, taking ceiling halves in place, taking floor halves shifted one cell right, and adding gives exactly the formula for \(F\). Deleting trailing zeros does not change the zero-extended function. Consequently, the zero extension of the finite list after \(t\) steps is \(C_n^t\). Moreover, for \(n>0\), every iterated finite list is nonempty and its last entry is nonzero: this is true initially, and each step deletes all and only trailing zeros. Therefore, if its zero extension is \(U_n\), its length must be exactly \(n\) and every entry must be one. Thus
\[
\text{the finite list after }t\text{ steps is }[1,\ldots,1]
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C_n^t=U_n. \tag{8}
\]
It follows that
\[
a(n)=\min\{t:C_n^t=U_n\}. \tag{9}
\]
In particular,
\[
C_n^{a(n)}=U_n,
\qquad C_n^t\ne U_n\quad(t<a(n)). \tag{10}
\]

We now couple the processes of total masses \(n\) and \(n+1\). For a configuration \(c\) and position \(p\), write \(c+\delta_p\) for the configuration obtained by adding one unit at position \(p\). The elementary parity identities
\[
\left\lceil\frac{m+1}{2}\right\rceil
=
\left\lceil\frac m2\right\rceil+
\begin{cases}1,&m\text{ even},\\0,&m\text{ odd},\end{cases}
\]
and
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m+1}{2}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lfloor\frac m2\right\rfloor+
\begin{cases}0,&m\text{ even},\\1,&m\text{ odd}
\end{cases}
\]
show that
\[
F(c+\delta_p)=
\begin{cases}
Fc+\delta_p,&c(p)\text{ even},\\
Fc+\delta_{p+1},&c(p)\text{ odd}.
\end{cases} \tag{11}
\]
Thus the single extra unit stays at its current position when the underlying mass there is even, and moves one position right when that mass is odd.

Define its position \(p_n(t)\) by
\[
p_n(0)=0,
\qquad
p_n(t+1)=
\begin{cases}
p_n(t)+1,&C_n^t(p_n(t))\text{ odd},\\
p_n(t),&C_n^t(p_n(t))\text{ even}.
\end{cases} \tag{12}
\]
Since \(C_{n+1}^0=C_n^0+\delta_0\), induction using (11) yields the coupling identity
\[
C_{n+1}^t=C_n^t+\delta_{p_n(t)} \quad\text{for every }t. \tag{13}
\]

We need two bounds relating the extra particle to the leading string of ones.

First, as long as the mass-\(n\) process has not stabilized before time \(t\),
\[
p_n(t)<n. \tag{14}
\]
This follows by induction. The only way the inequality could first fail is if \(p_n(t)=n-1\) and the extra particle moves right. By (12), \(C_n^t(n-1)\) would then be odd and positive. The no-internal-zero property would make all first \(n\) cells positive. Since their total mass is exactly \(n\), each would have to equal one, and by (3) all later cells would be zero. That would say \(C_n^t=U_n\), contrary to the assumed nonstability at that time.

Second, whenever \(C_n^t\ne U_n\),
\[
L_n(t)\le p_n(t)+1. \tag{15}
\]
We prove this by induction on \(t\). At time zero, unless the state is already stable, its first cell is not one, so \(L_n(0)=0\), while \(p_n(0)=0\).

For the induction step, put \(L=L_n(t)\) and \(p=p_n(t)\). Every cell before \(L\) equals one. The update preserves those leading ones: for \(i<L\), both the relevant cell and, when \(i>0\), its left neighbor are one, so \((FC_n^t)(i)=1\). At cell \(L\), the incoming contribution from the left is zero when \(L=0\), and is \(\lfloor1/2\rfloor=0\) when \(L>0\). Hence
\[
C_n^{t+1}(L)=\left\lceil\frac{C_n^t(L)}2\right\rceil. \tag{16}
\]
By (5), \(C_n^t(L)\ge2\). If it is at least three, (16) is at least two, so the first non-one remains at \(L\):
\[
L_n(t+1)=L.
\]
The induction hypothesis and the fact that the extra particle either stays or moves right then give (15) at time \(t+1\).

The other possibility is \(C_n^t(L)=2\). Then (16) equals one. Provided the next state is not stable, its first non-one is exactly at \(L+1\). Indeed, if the old cell \(L+1\) is positive, then the new mass at \(L+1\) is at least
\(\lfloor2/2\rfloor=1\) from the left plus at least one retained from that positive cell, and so is at least two. If the old cell \(L+1\) is zero, then all later cells are zero; in that case the old state has the precise form
\[
(\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{L\text{ cells}},2,0,0,\ldots),
\]
and one more step is \(U_{L+2}\), so this is exactly the stable-next-state exception. Thus, in the nonstable-next-state case,
\[
L_n(t+1)=L+1. \tag{17}
\]
By induction, \(L\le p+1\). If already \(L\le p\), then (17) immediately gives \(L+1\le p+1\le p_n(t+1)+1\). The only delicate case is \(L=p+1\). Then \(p<L\), so \(C_n^t(p)=1\), which is odd; therefore the extra particle moves from \(p\) to \(p+1=L\). Again \(L_n(t+1)=L+1=p_n(t+1)+1\). This proves (15).

We also record the exact shape one step before stabilization. Suppose
\[
C_n^t\ne U_n,
\qquad C_n^{t+1}=U_n. \tag{18}
\]
Then
\[
L_n(t)=n-2,
\qquad C_n^t(L_n(t))=2,
\qquad C_n^t(i)=0\quad(i>L_n(t)). \tag{19}
\]
To prove this, put \(L=L_n(t)\). If \(C_n^t(L)\ge3\), (16) shows that the next state still has a non-one at \(L\), contradicting (18). Hence the leading non-one has mass exactly two. If \(C_n^t(L+1)>0\), then, as in the proof of (17), the next mass at \(L+1\) is at least two, again contradicting stability. Therefore \(C_n^t(L+1)=0\), and no internal zeros imply that every later cell is zero. The old state consequently consists of \(L\) leading ones followed by a two. Its total mass is \(L+2=n\), proving (19). A direct application of the update also confirms that this shape evolves to \(U_n\).

We can now locate the extra particle at the stabilization time
\[
T=a(n).
\]
We claim
\[
p_n(T)=n-1
\quad\text{or}\quad
\bigl(n\ge2\text{ and }p_n(T)=n-2\bigr). \tag{20}
\]
If \(T=0\), then \(C_n^0=U_n\), which for positive \(n\) forces \(n=1\), and \(p_n(0)=0=n-1\).

Assume now that \(T>0\). By minimality, \(C_n^{T-1}\ne U_n\), while \(C_n^T=U_n\). Formula (19) says, with \(L=L_n(T-1)\), that
\[
L=n-2,
\]
and the state at time \(T-1\) consists of \(L\) ones, then a two, then zeros. In particular \(n\ge2\). By (15),
\[
n-2=L\le p_n(T-1)+1,
\]
so \(p_n(T-1)\ge n-3\). By (14), \(p_n(T-1)<n\). Thus only the final three positions can be relevant.

If the mass at \(p_n(T-1)\) is odd, that position cannot be \(n-2\), where the mass is two, and cannot be \(n-1\), where the mass is zero. It is therefore the preceding position \(n-3\) (with the small boundary cases interpreted by the same inequalities), and the extra particle moves right to \(n-2\). If the mass at its position is even, the extra particle does not move. It cannot lie strictly before \(L=n-2\), because all such cells have mass one, which is odd. Hence it is at \(n-2\) or \(n-1\). In all cases its time-\(T\) position is \(n-2\) or \(n-1\), proving (20).

We need one more minimality observation. If \(C_n^t\ne U_n\), then
\[
C_{n+1}^t\ne U_{n+1}. \tag{21}
\]
Suppose to the contrary that (13) gives
\[
C_n^t+\delta_{p_n(t)}=U_{n+1}.
\]
The extra position must be below \(n+1\), since otherwise the first \(n+1\) entries of \(C_n^t\) would all be one, contradicting the fact that \(C_n^t(n)=0\). At the extra position, the underlying state must have value zero, while at every other position below \(n+1\) it has value one. If the extra position is \(n\), this says exactly that \(C_n^t=U_n\), contrary to assumption. If it is below \(n\), then the following cell is one while the extra position itself is zero, contradicting the no-internal-zero property. This proves (21).

We now finish the proof. Fix \(n\ge1\) and put \(T=a(n)\). From (10) and (13),
\[
C_{n+1}^T=U_n+\delta_{p_n(T)}. \tag{22}
\]
This is not yet \(U_{n+1}\): in either case of (20), the added unit lies below \(n\), so cell \(n\) is still zero. Moreover, for every \(t<T\), (10) and (21) show that \(C_{n+1}^t\ne U_{n+1}\). Therefore
\[
a(n+1)>T. \tag{23}
\]

There are two cases.

If \(p_n(T)=n-1\), the underlying cell in \(U_n\) has mass one, hence is odd. By the extra-particle rule (11), one step moves the extra unit from \(n-1\) to \(n\), while \(U_n\) itself remains fixed. Consequently
\[
F(U_n+\delta_{n-1})=U_n+\delta_n=U_{n+1}.
\]
Together with (22), this says that the mass-\(n+1\) process stabilizes at time \(T+1\). By (23) it did not stabilize at or before \(T\). Hence
\[
a(n+1)=T+1=a(n)+1.
\]

If instead \(n\ge2\) and \(p_n(T)=n-2\), the extra unit first moves from \(n-2\) to \(n-1\), because \(U_n(n-2)=1\) is odd:
\[
F(U_n+\delta_{n-2})=U_n+\delta_{n-1}.
\]
This intermediate configuration is not \(U_{n+1}\), since its cell \(n\) is still zero. On the following step the extra unit moves from \(n-1\) to \(n\), again because the underlying mass there is one, and so
\[
F^2(U_n+\delta_{n-2})=U_n+\delta_n=U_{n+1}.
\]
Thus the mass-\(n+1\) process is stable at time \(T+2\), but not at time \(T+1\); by (23), it was also not stable at any earlier time. Therefore
\[
a(n+1)=T+2=a(n)+2.
\]

The two cases exhaust (20). Hence for every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[
\boxed{\ a(n+1)-a(n)\in\{1,2\}\ },
\]
as required.
